extracted.intended_audience: members of Parliament/legislators, learned men, and the literate public concerned with press freedom and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay arguing why prior licensing/censorship of printed books is impractical, harmful to learning, and an affront to authors and the public; addressed to lawmakers and the educated public. It assembles principled and pragmatic objections to an order of licensing and offers standards for when law vs persuasion should be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineffectiveness of licensing to prevent learned corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of controversy in religion are more doubtful and dangerous to the learned than to the ignorant; yet licensing cannot prevent learned men from being tainted, and learned corruption easily spreads from learned to common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Arminius was reportedly perverted by reading a nameless discourse. The essay argues that learned men catch and spread heresy quickly, and that suppression of books will not stop corrupted teaching where teachers guide readers. Licensing therefore fails as a preventative measure against doctrinal corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensers would need near-infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If learned men are the first receivers and spreaders of books, then licensers must themselves be trusted above all others in the land — possessing 'the grace of infallibility and uncorruptedness' — to be relied on to distinguish safe from harmful works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is unrealistic; requiring such moral and intellectual perfection in licensers is unattainable and would produce grave mistakes or injustice in censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing is impracticable because it would require regulating all amusements
rubrics_metrics.description: To regulate books effectively would force regulators to police 'all recreation and pastimes' — music, dance, songs, garments, conversation, and other media by which morals are shaped — since these, like books, influence manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lists concrete impracticalities (licensed dancers, inspectors of instruments, forbidding airs and madrigals, licensing windows and balconies for frontispieces) to show that partial regulation of books is absurd unless one undertakes an impossible total regulation of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing books cannot remove vice and will also remove virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: They who imagine to remove sin by removing its matter (books) misunderstand human nature: banishing objects of lust or all books will not make people chaste or virtuous, because the same matter can produce both vice and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that removing stimulus expels both sin and the possibility to cultivate virtue; thus heavy-handed suppression is morally and practically misguided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing discourages and affronts learning and learned men
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a licenser's approval is the greatest discouragement and affront to authors and scholars; it treats serious writers as pupils under a guardian, dishonours their labour, and deters the free pursuit of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects include: loss of pride in authorship, fewer people willing to pursue study, and devaluation of scholarly labour. The essay emphasizes harm to both living and posthumous reputations when licensers expunge or alter works.

rubrics_metrics.name: The licenser's work is onerous and will attract unworthy appointees
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of reading and judging every book is tedious and time-consuming; few of worth will accept it, and those who do will be 'unleisured' and ill-suited, producing licensers who are ignorant, imperious, remiss, or pecuniary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the job requires constant, unchosen reading of lengthy or poor texts, it drains the time of competent scholars and invites lower-quality supervision, making censorship ineffective or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior authorization favors current orthodoxies and suppresses novel thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A licenser's office and commission incline him to 'let pass nothing but what is vulgarly received already,' thereby preventing bold or innovative statements and entrenching received opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cautionary examples: Galileo's punishment by the Inquisition; the possibility that even great dead authors (e.g., Knox) would have bold sentences struck out. Licensing, therefore, curtails intellectual progress and silences important dissenting voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint treats the public as incapable and offends the laity
rubrics_metrics.description: If people cannot be trusted with an English pamphlet without a licenser, this implicitly judges them giddy, vicious, and ungrounded — a reproach to the common people and an alignment with 'popish' disdain for the laity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undermines respect for the public's capacity for judgment and parallels repressive practices in places where laity are 'most hated and despised.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing promotes intellectual laziness among clergy and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the press is curbed and bold books cannot issue forth, ministers and readers may rest on a ready stock of printed sermons and collections, reducing incentive to study, exercise, and keep watch over received opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, freedom to publish forces ministers and scholars to remain vigilant and to defend and improve their teachings; censorship risks producing a culture of complacency and rote repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishing and forbidding writings can increase their authority and spawn sects
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting writings can act as a 'nursing-mother to sects' because punished writings gain in reputation; a forbidden writing is thought to be a spark of truth, which enhances the punished author's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore suppression may backfire politically and socially, fostering the very schisms it aims to prevent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing dishonours authors and undermines authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: To distrust the judgment of an author and require his book to be examined and signed by a licenser is a 'displeasure and indignity' that places the author under wardship, detracting from his honour and standing in the Commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include: authors treated as pupils, inhibited revisions (press must follow licensed copy), thwarted additions to works, and the chilling of sincere publication—especially harmful for diligent writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing requires an immense administrative apparatus (cataloguing, expurgation, printer policing)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be effective, the Order would require repealing and proscribing existing scandalous books, cataloguing condemned works, expurgating partly culpable books, and forbidding printers with suspected typography — duties demanding many overseers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns this would emulate the models of Trent and Seville (Inquisition systems), which are detested; the administrative cost and moral hazard make such a system undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law should only restrain clearly punishable matters; persuasion and education should govern the rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish what the law ought to 'bid restraint and punishment' upon and what should be addressed by 'persuasion only' — unwritten laws of virtuous education and nurture are the true sustainers of a commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advocates for virtuous education, civil nurture, and persuasion as effective means; the law should not overreach into areas it cannot rightly and usefully regulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of publication enables public refutation and the exercise of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is more public than preaching and 'more easy to refutation'; open publication allows challengers and champions of truth to refute and defend opinions, exercising communal judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus free writing contributes to the progress of knowledge by making claims visible and contestable; restricting publication removes this beneficial public testing of ideas.
